crosswalk.note: Uplift RCTs, pilot→production and app-layer margin net of inference measure the same valve.
Deployment/FDE services capture part of the surplus that adaptation creates.
Adaptation measured inside deployed products: regulated devices built on language models and paid robotaxi rides.

description: The products people use and the firms that put AI to work: coding assistants, apps built for one industry, consumer apps, AI-native firms that sell finished work, firms that train the people who deploy AI, and firms that buy up service businesses to run them with AI.

economics.case: Palantir's filing describes the route from services to software. It sells platforms that connect a customer's data and operations to large language models (the kind of AI model that reads and writes text) made by other firms; its software engineers working with existing customers run deployments and look for new uses; and it runs short workshops, which it calls bootcamps, that build working tools on a customer's own data within days. It also warns that pilots (trial projects) given at little or no cost may never turn into paying contracts. Much of its revenue comes from existing customers widening their use, and the average revenue from its largest customers rose in 2025 over 2024. No single customer reached the size at which the filing must report it in any year from 2023 to 2025, though governments bring in much of its revenue, and it names large software firms, government contractors and systems integrators (firms that assemble other companies' technology for a client) among its rivals. The labs are buying this layer: this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI agreeing to buy Tomoro as it launched the Deployment Company, and the Deployment Company agreeing to buy Northslope, both consultancies that put AI to work in large firms; and Poolside, a lab, buying Fern Labs, a deployment firm. This site's records also hold the Anthropic venture buying Fractional AI and Casper Studios, firms that build AI systems for clients; the record of acquisitions leaves those two out of its count under its written rules, because no single buyer controls the venture. Whether the work pays off is unsettled: in one survey of large firms, most AI pilots built into their systems showed no measurable effect on profit, though another survey, which counts differently, finds many more reaching everyday use.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that generic integration, wiring a model to a firm's documents and common business software, is becoming a commodity: the clouds and labs ship connectors (links that let a model read and act in other software) and tools for building agents (AI programs that carry out tasks on their own), and each new model needs less hand-fitting. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets. This site judges that the deployer owns neither the model nor the customer's records, so on generic work it earns an ordinary services return.
economics.converts_if: A deployer's work ends in its own platform, which the customer's operations come to run on, so replacing it means rebuilding the work, not repointing it: switching costs in Helmer's sense. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Williamson would add that a lab owning the deployer keeps its model inside that platform, which is why the labs are buying consultancies. The rent stays with services margins if the models learn to fit themselves to a firm's work.
economics.kill_shot: Deployment firms keeping or widening their margins while the models need less fitting with each release and the labs give deployment away to win model sales; or, the other way, deployment staff becoming easy to hire while customers still stay with the firm that first fitted their systems.
economics.mechanism: Deployment firms send engineers into a customer to connect AI models to its data, systems and daily work. The industry calls them forward-deployed engineers: staff who sit with the customer rather than at head office. This site judges Palantir the largest listed firm doing this work, though Palantir describes itself as selling software platforms. The labs have set up their own deployment arms, among them the OpenAI Deployment Company and a venture Anthropic formed with Blackstone and other investors (reports in this site's records differ on who the others are) to serve companies owned by private-equity firms (investment firms that buy whole companies); and consultancies sell the same work. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input here is people who understand both the models and the customer's business, and that selling their hours earns a wage-like margin, because each new customer needs more of them. Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts, found that an asset built for one buyer, worth far less anywhere else, ties that buyer to whoever holds it. This site judges that the rent appears only when the deployment leaves behind such an asset: software and a map of the customer's data that its work comes to run on.

rival.title: Engineers who fit AI to each firm are the scarce ingredient

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is engineers who can turn a firm's messy data and unwritten habits into working systems, and, once that is done, the map of the customer's data and operations that the system runs on. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the likeliest here, and Palantir's expanding customers fit them, but its filing reports expansion, not how many customers leave, so this site does not count the power proven. The rival view holds that these engineers are scarce enough to collect a scarcity rent themselves, not a wage-like margin.
economics.title: Fitting AI into a firm earns a services margin that grows with headcount; a rent lasts only where the deployer leaves behind software the customer runs its work on

economics.case: Coding agents hold large and fast-rising run-rates (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) in this site's records. Cursor's grew sharply between February and June 2026 on press reports citing people close to it; Cognition says its own grew sharply between May and September 2026; and Anthropic said, in announcing a funding round early in 2026, that Claude Code's had grown sharply since the year began. The last two are company figures, not audited ones. This site holds no comparable readings for OpenAI's Codex or for GitHub's tools, though its record of acquisitions shows the teams of small coding-tool firms joining OpenAI's Codex division in 2025 and 2026. The labs and their owners are buying in. SpaceX took an option in April 2026 to buy Cursor for its own shares, and Cursor says the purchase was completed in August. SpaceX's quarterly filing says that alongside the option it agreed to give Cursor computing capacity and to work with it on improving xAI's Grok models and developing new ones jointly; that August Cursor released a Grok model it says the two built together. Cursor says the deal gives it SpaceX's fleet of GPUs (the chips AI runs on) to train stronger models that cost less to run; it had said in late 2025 that its in-house models already wrote a great deal of code. Lovable says it draws on several models, matching each part of a job to the one best suited to it, and tunes open-source models (free code anyone may use and change) of its own. Cognition names large firms, NVIDIA and Citi among them, whose engineering teams use its agent. Google hired away Windsurf's leaders in July 2025 and Cognition agreed to buy the rest of the firm; this site's record of acquisitions also shows OpenAI and Anthropic hiring the teams of smaller coding-tool firms. Microsoft's filing describes GitHub as a platform where developers add AI and agent tools across the whole of building software. Each use costs an app the model's price, which a classic software firm does not pay: ICONIQ, an investment firm, puts the gross margin (sales minus the direct cost of making them, as a share of sales) of the AI products in its survey at [fact:ai_app_margin]. Whether the agents make developers faster is less clear than their revenue suggests: randomised trials (tests that compare groups assigned by chance) by METR, a research group, have not found developers working faster with AI tools, and METR calls the evidence from its newer trial weak.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that the agent's wrapper, the editor, the chat window and the loop that lets a model run and test code, is becoming a commodity: several sellers offer much the same, open-source versions exist, and the labs bundle their own with their models. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that the firm holding the scarce inputs a product needs usually keeps the profit; here the lab holds the model, the scarcest input.
economics.converts_if: An agent becomes the place a firm's software is planned, reviewed and run, holding its rules, permissions and history, so leaving means rebuilding how its engineers work: switching costs in Helmer's sense. Or its record of developers' corrections trains models of its own good enough to cut what it pays the labs. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the owners of models to bring the agents inside, as SpaceX did with Cursor.
economics.kill_shot: An independent coding agent keeping its customers and its margin through a year in which the labs cut their own agents' prices and ship better models to everyone at once, with customers not moving to the labs' tools.
economics.mechanism: A coding agent is an AI tool that writes, edits and tests software, from suggesting the next line to carrying out a whole task on its own. The independent sellers include Cognition, Replit, Lovable, Factory and Augment. The labs and their owners sell their own: Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, and Cursor, made by Anysphere, which SpaceX, the owner of the lab xAI, bought in 2026 and which now works with xAI on its Grok models; and Microsoft sells coding tools through GitHub, a site where developers keep and share code. This site judges that the independent agents mostly run on models bought from the labs, paying by the token (a fragment of a word), though some train models of their own. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input in a coding agent is the model underneath, which the labs own, so an independent agent keeps a rent only for what it adds: its editor (the program in which developers write and read code), its grip on a firm's code and habits, and its own models where it trains them.

rival.title: Apps keep their margin through what they build around the model

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the best coding model at any moment, and, for an agent maker, the record of how developers accept, reject and correct its work, which could train its own models. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; a record of accepted code may pass the first and last tests, but goes stale as models improve. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the candidate, but this site judges that a firm can try a rival agent alongside the one it has, and no seller publishes figures on customers leaving, so this site does not count them proven.
economics.title: Coding agents are among the fastest-growing AI apps, but the labs sell their own and a lab's owner now holds Cursor; an independent agent's margin is a lease on the labs' models

economics.case: Several of these firms report revenue rising fast. Harvey's co-founder said in September 2026 that its annual recurring revenue (what customers have signed up to pay in a year) had grown sharply since January; Legora's chief executive describes the same kind of rise; Decagon told a reporter in August 2026 that its revenue had crossed a large milestone, and a research firm estimates that its run-rate (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) rose sharply from the end of 2025; and a research firm estimates that OpenEvidence's run-rate rose sharply between the end of 2025 and July 2026. All of these are company, press or research-firm figures, not audited ones. The apps are building their own assets: Harvey said in September 2026 that it had released its first open-weight model (one whose trained settings are published) tuned for legal work, and that it aims to help law firms build AI they own. OpenEvidence has content partnerships with the New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and the American Medical Association; it gave its research agent free to verified American clinicians in 2025, and it said in March 2026 that most practising American physicians use it every day. Menlo Ventures, a venture-capital firm (one that invests in young companies), found in its survey that start-ups took [fact:startup_app_share] of what American firms spent on AI apps, though the survey leaves out AI built into incumbents' existing software. The labs and platforms are moving into the same trades. Anthropic said early in 2026 that its Cowork product has plugins (add-ons that give its model the tools and instructions for one job) for roles such as sales, legal and finance, and that it had widened its reach into health care; Microsoft's filing describes a cloud business, once called Nuance Healthcare, that sells AI to the health care industry; and this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI buying Torch, a health-care technology start-up, in January 2026. The same record shows labs and platforms buying vertical apps: Mistral bought Emmi AI and agreed to buy Pimento, OpenAI bought Crixet, Microsoft bought Fintool and Amazon bought NLX. Where the work is regulated, rules slow everyone: a start-up, UpDoc, said in December 2025 that the Food and Drug Administration had given its diabetes app the first clearance for medical software using large language models that talk to patients, though the agency's own record of the clearance does not describe it that way. Harvey's own test of expert legal work found the best general models finishing few of its tasks end to end in May 2026, a vendor's test not yet repeated by anyone else.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that a vertical app that adds only prompts (the written instructions given to a model) and a trade's vocabulary to a general model is becoming a commodity, since each general release learns more trades at once. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a clever way of asking a model a legal question is information of that kind.
economics.converts_if: A vertical app becomes the system of record for its trade, the software that holds a firm's matters, patients or cases, so switching costs in Helmer's sense hold customers when the labs catch up; or a regulator's approval, or the trade's liability rules, make the app's checked record something a lab cannot simply match, turning its rent into a regulated one. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the labs to keep buying the apps whose trades they want.
economics.kill_shot: Vertical apps' prices and margins falling each time the labs release a better general model, with customers switching to the labs' own specialist products; or, the other way, a vertical app keeping its customers and prices after a lab ships a rival product for the same trade.
economics.mechanism: Vertical AI apps are built for one trade: Harvey and Legora for lawyers, OpenEvidence, Abridge and Ambience for doctors, Hebbia and Rogo for finance, Sierra and Decagon for customer service. They buy models from the labs and wrap them in the forms, checks and records of one kind of work. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that the profit often goes to whoever holds the complementary assets: the distribution, the trade's trust and the systems a product needs to reach its buyers. This site judges that a vertical app earns a rent only where it holds such assets that a lab cannot copy by training a better general model.

rival.title: Apps that resell the labs' models get squeezed

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the place in the trade's daily work (the tool a lawyer drafts in or a doctor's notes are written by), the trade's own records the app is allowed to see, licensed content the trade trusts, such as the medical journals OpenEvidence draws on, and approvals that only a regulator or a licensed professional can give. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; much of a trade's data belongs to each client and helps only that client. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) and branding (buyers paying more because of the name) are the candidates, but these firms are young and publish no figures on customers leaving, so this site counts neither proven.
economics.title: A trade's own AI app keeps a rent where it holds the trade's workflow, records and approvals; where it only packages a general model, each lab release takes the margin

economics.case: The platforms are putting AI where their users already are. Meta's filing says Meta AI is available across its apps, as a stand-alone app, on its AI glasses and on the web, and that Meta earns substantially all its revenue from advertising. Google's filing says its Gemini model runs across Search and the Gemini app, and warns that as AI enters Search it may earn money differently than it has in the past. OpenAI reaches consumers through ChatGPT directly; its paying subscribers stand at [fact:paid_share] of its weekly users on this site's latest reading, two different counts, so this is not the share of users who pay. The owners of habits are buying small consumer apps: this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI buying Roi, Torch, Hiro Finance and NextSlide, Meta buying Manus and Limitless, and Amazon agreeing to buy Bee. Users are getting much of the value: Stanford's Digital Economy Lab estimated what American users would have to be paid to give up generative AI (AI that writes text or makes images on request), and its total rose sharply between the middle of 2025 and early 2026; the survey counts only Americans. This site holds no revenue readings for the companion apps. A wave of personal agents arrived in 2026. Meta says its Muse, launched in September 2026, runs in a sandbox of its own (a separate computer in Meta's cloud, walled off from other users, with its own web browser), books travel, fills in forms and buys things, checks with the user before it sends an email or makes a purchase, and pays through Link, a checkout service built by Stripe; Meta also says Muse is free for most uses with paid plans for more, and does not share users' conversations with Muse, or the data in their Muse workspace, with its ad systems. Instinct, a start-up whose users text it, and whose concierge feature makes phone calls for them, uses its own phone number and computer to carry out tasks, TechCrunch reported when it raised a new round in September 2026 from investors including Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Coatue, a month after its previous one. Manus, whose makers describe it as a general-purpose agent for research and complex tasks, announced in December 2025 that it was joining Meta. Assistant Benchmark, a site that tests assistants people can text on the same published tasks, ranked Muse first and Instinct second in its tests as of September 2026; the site, created by David Pawlan, says it scored the assistants it tested after real use; it had tested only some of those it lists, so these are one site's results, not a survey of users.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that answering an everyday question is a commodity: many free assistants do it well enough, and the price to the user is zero. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to users as lower prices and better products. On his finding, the gap between what users would pay and what they are charged is the value they keep. The rival view holds that the labs are durable, high-margin businesses whose customers mostly do not switch, which would leave more of the value with the makers.
economics.converts_if: An assistant's memory of each user becomes costly to leave, turning a habit into switching costs in Helmer's sense (what a user would lose by moving to a rival); or assistants learn what people want to buy early enough that advertisers pay more to reach them than in search, turning attention into the kind of rent search earned. It fails to convert if memories become easy to carry from one assistant to another. A third route opens with agents that buy for their users: the agent becomes the place where payment happens, and its owner takes a fee on each purchase, a rent on the sale rather than on attention. That fails to convert if users can move their saved cards, logins and preferences to a rival agent easily, or if shops and payment firms such as Stripe keep the fee.
economics.kill_shot: A consumer AI app with no existing platform behind it, such as a personal agent like Instinct, taking a large, paying audience from Meta, Google and ChatGPT and holding it; or consumer AI firms' revenue growing as fast as the value users say they get.
economics.mechanism: Consumer AI is the assistants and apps people use for themselves: OpenAI's ChatGPT, Meta AI inside Meta's apps, Google's Gemini in its app and in Search, Perplexity's answer engine, and companion apps such as Character.AI and Replika, which act as a friend or partner. Many people use them free; some pay a subscription, and advertising may pay for the rest. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that in consumer AI the scarce input is a user's habit, the app someone opens without thinking, and that it is held by firms that already own people's phones, feeds and searches, plus ChatGPT, which built one of its own. A newer kind of consumer AI, the personal agent (an assistant that carries out tasks for its user, such as booking, shopping, filling in forms and paying, rather than only answering), adds a second question beside the habit: who stands where the user pays.

rival.title: The labs are durable businesses with high margins

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the user's attention and habit, the personal history an assistant builds up about each user, and the payment and advertising systems that turn attention into money. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called those inputs complementary assets; Meta and Google held theirs before AI arrived. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Network economies (each user makes the product more useful to the others) and scale economies hold in the platforms' existing businesses, but this site finds none proven for AI assistants themselves, where one user's chat does not make another's better and people use several at once. This site judges that agents which act, not just answer, could move both the habit and the point of payment: if people hand their errands to one agent, the firm running it stands between them and every shop they buy from, and could take a cut of each purchase, as card networks and app stores do, or charge sellers to be chosen. Whether that rent goes to the platforms that already own the habit, such as Meta with Muse and Manus, or to newcomers such as Instinct is open; one tester's early rankings are not evidence of lasting use. Because Meta says Muse keeps users' conversations with it, and the data in their Muse workspace, out of its ad systems, this site judges that, for now, the source suggests any money Muse makes would come from subscriptions or purchases rather than advertising.
economics.title: In consumer AI the rent goes to whoever owns the daily habit, and users keep most of the value

economics.case: This site holds no revenue or margin readings for any AI rollup; the evidence is structural. The site's automatability census, which screens tasks for whether their shape would let them be handed to software, asks of each trade whether its owner would keep the saving, and answers from how the trade sends its bills. Where the bill counts hours, as in most accounting and audit work, cutting the time cuts the bill and the client keeps the saving, which is why the census calls accounting its false positive. Where the fee is set by something other than the firm's own costs, such as a share of a placed candidate's salary, a commission on a booking or a fixed fee set by the payer, the owner can keep it until the price is next reset. The labs are reaching the same buyers another way: OpenAI has set up the OpenAI Deployment Company, which is buying consultancies that put AI to work in large firms, and Anthropic has formed a venture with Blackstone and other investors (reports in this site's records differ on who the others are) to serve companies that private-equity firms (investment firms that buy whole companies) own. This site's entry for General Catalyst's plan rests on a press report not yet confirmed by a second source.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that the AI a rollup uses is bought from the labs and software firms like any other customer's, so it gives no lasting edge over a rival firm that buys the same tools. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. In a trade where clients re-bid their contracts, a saving becomes a lower price once rivals match it. The rival view holds that AI lets one centre see and run many unrelated businesses, an edge that would outlast the tools themselves.
economics.converts_if: A rollup turns its running of many firms into a way of working rivals take years to learn, what Helmer calls process power, or grows large enough in one trade and place that its costs per client fall below any single firm's, his scale economies. Both need the saving to outlast the next time clients re-bid, which in trades billed by the hour means moving clients to fixed fees first.
economics.kill_shot: AI rollups in trades billed by the hour keeping higher margins for years after buying, without moving clients to fixed fees; or rollups' margins falling back to their trades' ordinary level as rivals that did not merge buy the same AI tools.
economics.mechanism: A rollup buys many small firms in one trade, such as accounting, property management or home services, and runs them as one. The groups this site files as AI rollups, among them Thrive Holdings, Long Lake, Crete, Dwelly and Titan, and funds such as General Catalyst that have set money aside to build them, plan to run the firms they buy with AI and keep the saving. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who studied contracts and found that whoever depends on an asset owned by someone else can be squeezed by its owner, would read a rollup as a bet that owning the customer, the licence and the trust is worth more than selling software to the firm that owns them. This site judges that the bet pays only where the firm's prices do not fall when its costs do.
economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the customer relationship, a licence or professional's signature where the trade needs one, and prices that are set by something other than the firm's costs. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called such inputs complementary assets and found that their owners often keep the profit; the rollup buys them rather than building them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for any AI rollup yet.
economics.title: A rollup keeps AI's saving only where the firms it buys are paid for results rather than hours; its asset is the customer, and the AI is bought in

profiles.customers: Advertisers pay for substantially all of it, the 10-K says. It also says most of its revenue comes from marketers advertising on Facebook and Instagram, that they make no long-term commitments, and that the loss of marketers or cuts in their spending could seriously harm the business. It names no large customer. The users it reaches are counted in billions of daily visitors, a figure Meta measures itself and warns may be inaccurate. Meta AI earns no direct revenue that the 10-K reports. This site judges the paying base is diffuse, spread across many advertisers.
profiles.disclosure: Drafted by a Claude model, made by Anthropic, which competes with, sells to or buys from companies in this layer; Alex Brogan reviews this profile before it is relied on.
profiles.market: Meta runs Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp and Threads, and its 10-K (the annual report US companies file with their regulator) says it earns substantially all its revenue from advertising on those apps. Its AI work sits on both sides of that business. It builds its own models, including the Llama family, which it has released openly in the past; the 10-K says it expects to train a mix of open and closed models from here (an open model is one whose trained settings are published so anyone can run it). It offers Meta AI, an assistant available inside its apps, as a stand-alone app, on its AI glasses and on the web. And it uses AI to choose which posts and ads each person sees, which the 10-K credits with better ad targeting and measurement. It states a goal of building superintelligence, which it defines as AI that surpasses human intelligence. To pay for this it spends heavily on data centres: this site's records from its filings show its capital spending (money spent on buildings and machines) growing much faster than its revenue in 2025 and again so far in 2026, and its 10-K lists large commitments, mostly for data centres and for computing capacity rented from other firms. In October 2025 it entered an arrangement to co-develop a data-centre campus in Louisiana, in which it holds a minority interest. In June 2025 it bought a non-voting minority stake in Scale AI, a seller of training data made by people; its filings say it has no significant influence over Scale's operations, and Scale's founder joined Meta to work on its AI. This site's records also hold Meta buying Manus and Limitless in December 2025 and Stilla in September 2026, and buying or hiring teams from other small AI firms in March 2026. Manus, maker of a general-purpose AI agent (software that carries out tasks such as research and building things for its user, rather than only answering), announced in December 2025 that it was joining Meta, and said it would keep selling its own subscriptions and operating from Singapore. In September 2026 Meta launched Muse, a personal agent that Meta says runs in its own walled-off computer in Meta's cloud with its own web browser, books travel, fills in forms and buys things after checking with the user, pays through Link, a checkout service built by Stripe, is free for most uses with paid plans for more, and does not share users' conversations with Muse, or the data in their Muse workspace, with Meta's ad systems. The question is whether AI adds to or eats into the advertising business that pays for it.
must_be_true: Advertising keeps paying for the AI build-out. The 10-K says its AI work will need more spending on infrastructure and staff, and this site's records show capital spending rising far faster than revenue; ad revenue must keep growing fast enough to carry those costs and the losses of Reality Labs, its glasses and headsets division, which the 10-K says depends on profits earned elsewhere.

AI keeps making its ads work better, so advertisers keep paying more per ad; the 10-K reports more ads shown and a higher average price per ad in 2025, and credits its AI with better targeting and measurement.

People keep turning to Meta AI inside apps they already use rather than moving their questions, shopping and time to assistants from OpenAI or Google. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep, found that most goes to users; this site judges a free assistant only pays Meta if the attention it holds can be sold to advertisers.
Its own models stay close enough to the best to power its products, so it need not pay rival labs for the capability; the 10-K lists competitors whose AI may be better or cheaper among its risks.

Regulators let it keep showing personalised ads. The 10-K says the European Commission ruled in April 2025 that its offer of a paid subscription with no ads did not comply with EU rules, a decision it has appealed.

Its minority stake in Scale AI, which carries no vote, and its purchases of small AI firms add skills and products without drawing new limits from competition authorities, whose past scrutiny of its acquisitions the 10-K describes.

People let Muse act for them, booking and buying rather than only chatting, and Meta earns from that work through subscriptions or a share of what Muse buys, since Meta says Muse keeps users' conversations with it, and the data in their Muse workspace, out of its ad systems; for now, the source suggests, that leaves subscriptions and purchases rather than advertising. This site judges that an agent shopping for its user could draw spending away from the ads that pay Meta today, so the agent must earn at least what it displaces.

Manus, the agent maker that joined Meta in December 2025, adds skills and users to Meta's own agents; Manus said at the deal that it hoped to bring its subscription to the businesses and people on Meta's platforms.

powers.why: Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their rivals, found that a lasting advantage needs both a benefit and a barrier to copying. In Meta's social apps the benefit is that each user makes the apps more useful to friends and more valuable to advertisers; the barrier is that a rival must assemble a comparable audience first. The 10-K shows the audience still growing in 2025, with more ads shown and a higher average price per ad, so this site counts the power proven in its social apps. It finds no evidence yet that the power extends to Meta AI itself, where one person's chat does not improve another's.

Emerging, not proven. This site judges that the cost of training models and building ad-ranking systems is spread over Meta's very large audience and ad sales, so each user costs it less than a smaller rival; but the barrier holds only against newcomers, not against Google or the frontier labs (the firms building the most capable AI systems), which spend at similar scale and are its main AI rivals.

Emerging, not proven. Counter-positioning is a newcomer's model the incumbent could copy only by damaging its own business. The benefit is that Meta can give AI away inside its apps and let advertising pay; the barrier is that a lab living on subscriptions and paid access to its models would give up that revenue by doing the same. But the labs can add advertising too, and Meta AI has no revenue the 10-K reports, so this site does not count the barrier as proven.

profiles.market: Palantir sells software platforms that connect a large organisation's data to its daily operations, and its 10-K (the annual report US companies file with their regulator) names four: Gotham, Foundry, Apollo and AIP. AIP, its AI platform, connects customers securely to large language models (AI systems trained on huge amounts of text) made by other firms, and gives them tools to build agents (AI programs that carry out tasks on their own) on top. At the heart of its software is what it calls the Ontology, a map of how a customer's data relates to its real operations. It runs short workshops, which it calls bootcamps, that build working tools on a customer's own data within days, and it says it embeds its staff directly with customers. It warns that pilots given at little or no cost may never turn into paying contracts. Government customers brought in most of its revenue in 2025 and commercial customers the rest, and its revenue from US commercial customers rose steeply that year. How big the market becomes depends on whether fitting AI to a firm's operations stays a job for a software platform like Palantir's, or passes to the labs (the firms building the most capable AI systems), which have set up deployment arms of their own.
must_be_true: Its platform, not the model, stays where customers' work runs. AIP uses models made by others; this site judges that helps Palantir while the models are interchangeable, and hurts it if one lab's model becomes the product customers ask for by name.

The labs' own deployment arms do not take its commercial customers. This site's records hold the OpenAI Deployment Company agreeing to buy Tomoro in May 2026 and Northslope in July 2026, both firms that put AI to work inside large companies, and Poolside, a lab, buying Fern Labs, a deployment firm, in November 2025. David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns, found that profit tends to go to whoever holds the assets a product needs to reach buyers; here that is the customer relationship and the map of its data, which this site judges Palantir holds today for its own customers, and which the labs' deployment arms are trying to win.

Its margins hold as it sends more staff into customers. Its contribution margin, its own measure of revenue left after the cost of serving and winning customers, rose in both its government and commercial segments in 2025. This site judges that a business that must grow its engineers with each customer earns a services margin (the thinner margin of a firm that sells its staff's time) rather than a software margin (the wider one of a firm that sells the same code again at little extra cost).
Its short pilots and bootcamps keep turning into long, paid contracts, which the 10-K warns may not happen.

Governments and its other largest customers keep renewing their contracts, although many can be ended at will, budgets can stall, and the 10-K warns that a limited number of customers carry a substantial portion of its revenue.

profiles.market: Apple designs and sells the iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables and home devices, and sells services on them: the App Store, cloud storage, subscriptions, advertising, AppleCare and payments. Its 10-K (the annual report US companies file with their regulator), for the year to September 2025, says it designs nearly the entire solution for its products, from hardware and operating system to apps and services, and relies on outsourcing partners, mostly in Asia, to build them. The 10-K mentions artificial intelligence mainly among its risks: safety, copyright and regulation. Apple's machine-learning research site describes the models behind Apple Intelligence, its AI features: a small model that runs on the device itself, tuned for the chips Apple designs (Apple silicon), and a larger model that runs on Private Cloud Compute, Apple's own server platform, which it presents as part of its commitment to users' privacy. Apple says both models match or beat open models of similar size (models whose trained settings are published so anyone can run them); that is its own test, and a comparison with models of similar size, not with the frontier models (the most capable AI systems, from firms such as OpenAI and Google). The market map this site uses places Apple in edge inference: running a trained model on the user's own device rather than in a data centre. This site judges that Apple's AI market is not selling AI itself but keeping people on its devices and in its services: the 10-K shows its Services gross margin (the share of sales left after the direct cost of providing them) far above its Products gross margin, and rising again in 2025. How big this becomes depends on whether AI makes people buy new devices and stay in its services, or moves their daily habit to assistants that live in other companies' apps.
must_be_true: AI makes people keep buying and replacing its devices and keeps them in its services; the 10-K says competitors imitate its features and cut prices aggressively, and that Apple holds a minority share of the global markets for smartphones, personal computers, tablets and wearables.

Running AI on the device stays good enough for everyday requests, so that its own chips, rather than rented data-centre chips, carry most of the work; Apple compares its small model with open models of similar size, not with the frontier models.

When a request needs a stronger model than its own, Apple keeps the user inside its own interface and on its own terms, rather than users opening ChatGPT, Google's Gemini or another lab's app directly.

Its revenue from letting Google and others offer search on its devices survives the remedies a US court ordered against Google in September 2025; the 10-K says that order may still change in further proceedings or on appeal, and that a reversal on appeal could bring remedies barring Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search placement. This site judges it must also survive any shift of people's questions from search to AI assistants.

Courts and regulators leave it room to charge on its App Store; the 10-K describes a US court order barring it from charging a commission on certain purchases and a fine from the European Commission in April 2025 under the EU's Digital Markets Act. This site judges that if AI agents (assistants that act for their users, booking and buying) become where people pay, Apple keeps a share only while those purchases still pass through its devices and store.

Its suppliers keep delivering; the 10-K says it relies on single-source partners for many components, some of them custom parts available from only one source, and on partners in Asia for final assembly of substantially all its hardware.
profiles.name: Apple

powers.why: Emerging, not proven. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their rivals, required each lasting advantage to have both a benefit and a barrier to copying. The 10-K describes the loop: customers' decisions to buy its hardware depend in part on third-party apps, and developers weigh Apple's market position and expected sales when deciding whether to build for it. It does not show the barrier: it says its minority share of the global smartphone, computer, tablet and wearables markets can push developers toward rivals with larger shares, and that some rivals have large bases of active devices of their own. This site judges that the benefit shows in a Services gross margin far above its Products margin, but the filing does not tie that margin to the loop. Under the site's written rules that makes Apple's rent (profit above what it would earn in a fully competitive market) a scarcity rent, one that lasts while an input is short or a firm is first, and its durability short until a filing shows the barrier. This site finds no evidence that the loop extends to AI features, where one person's use does not improve another's.

Emerging, not proven. This site judges that an assistant which knows a user's messages, photos and habits on the device could make leaving costly. The barrier is untested: the 10-K reports no AI revenue or use, and assistants from other firms can run on the same phone.

would_disprove: Its Services gross margin falling for several years in a row.
Device sales falling, or people keeping their phones longer, after its AI features launch.
Its own models falling so far behind that it hands most AI requests to another firm's model, with that firm's brand shown to the user and much of the value paid to it.
Appeals ending with Google barred from offering Apple commercial terms for search placement, or search revenue shrinking as people ask AI assistants instead.
Regulators forcing it to allow other app stores and payment systems widely enough that its store commission falls.
